sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce Gen4P, a unified framework for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video. We show that a pretrained video generator can be repurposed into a feed-forward 4D perceiver without iterative denoising. Building on on-demand querying, Gen4P processes clean video latents in a single encoder pass and predicts the requested 4D attributes through a lightweight cross-attention decoder. The on-demand query formulation enables flexible spatial sampling, and our proposed continuous-time queries further provide temporal flexibility. To strengthen geometric knowledge, we propose a straightforward plug-in solution by incorporating a pretrained video-depth LoRA as a frozen geometry prior, improving overall performance without adding extra trainable parameters. Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on tasks of 3D point tracking, video depth and camera pose estimation. Qualitative results on in-the-wild videos illustrate its capability of tracking complex motion while maintaining the delicate structure. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception. See https://gen4p.github.io for more visual results.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: We consider the problem of feed-forward full 4D reconstruction from monocular video. unified 4D representation of scene geometry, depth, camera poses, and 3D point trajectories provides foundation for simulating and interacting with the physical environment. However, recovering such representation remains challenging: it requires accurately capturing both the static geometry and the dynamic motion of the scene across viewpoints and over time. Recent advances in feed-forward reconstruction demonstrate the value of pretrained foundational vision models. Geometry Foundation Models (GFMs), including VGGT (Wang et al., 2025a), VGGTΩ (Wang et al., 2026a), and DA3 (Lin et al., 2025), build on pretrained vision models (Oquab et al., 2023; Simeoni et al., 2025), adapting them through large-scale geometric supervision. These GFMs

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: then provide strong geometry priors for subsequent 4D reconstruction: V-DPM (Sucar et al., 2026) and 4RC (Luo et al., 2026), for instance, extend VGGT and DA3 to jointly recover geometry and motion. However, geometry priors alone do not explicitly model how points should evolve over time in dynamic scenes. Meanwhile, foundational generative models offer complementary source of priors over appearance, geometry, and motion, by learning to synthesize images and videos (Wan et al., 2025; ByteDance Seed Team, 2026). Recent studies have exploited generative priors for 2D correspondence (Hedlin et al., 2023), depth estimation (Ke et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025), 3D geometry recovery (Zhang et al., 2025b; Lu et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025), motion tracking (Zhu et al., 2026; Nam et al., 2026a), and general perception (Wang et al., 2026b). However, they still address 4D perception through task-specific approaches. Besides, they often require dense, frame-aligned supervision, limiting their flexibility in handling arbitrary spatiotemporal video inputs. In this work, we introduce Gen4P, 4D perceiver that leverages rich priors from large-scale pretrained video generators for full 4D reconstruction. Specifically, Gen4P tames multi-step video generator into single-step feed-forward 4D perceiver. To this end, the objective is formulated as learning direct regression network, instead of the iterative denoising for geometric reconstruction in prior works (Ke et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025). Such formulation requires only one encoder forward pass per input clip. The resulting scene tokens are then shared across queries, reducing the encoding cost over repeated 4D predictions. We obtain the full 4D attributes by querying the scene tokens using lightweight cross-attention decoder. It decouples the output sampling from pre-extracted feature grids, allowing spatial flexibility in the output resolution. Additionally, we introduce continuous-time query mechanism to handle variable-length video sequences effectively. Furthermore, we discover that pretrained video-depth LoRA can further be incorporated as frozen plug-in geometric prior, strengthening geometry without introducing additional trainable parameters. Our key contributions are summarized as follows: (i) we repurpose video generator into feedforward 4D perceiver under sparse query supervision, offering an alternative to GFM-based methods; (ii) we introduce continuous-time query mechanism together with on-demand decoding to provide temporal and spatial flexibility; (iii) we incorporate frozen depth LoRA as plug-in geometry prior, improving overall 4D reconstruction without adding trainable parameters; and (iv) we provide comprehensive evaluation of our method on set of 4D reconstruction tasks, complemented by qualitative results on in-the-wild videos, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalization.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Feed-forward GFMs directly regress pixel-aligned geometry, from pairwise point maps (Wang et al., 2024) to sequence models that use spatial memory (Wang & Agapito, 2025), recurrent scene states (Wang et al., 2025b), or joint multi-view attention with multiple prediction heads (Wang et al., 2025a). Later models remove the reference view (Wang et al., 2026c), accept optional geometric inputs (Keetha et al., 2026), or learn unified depthray targets (Lin et al., 2025). Point Tracking in 2D and 3D. 2D point tracking has been extensively studied in both sparse and dense settings (Doersch et al., 2022; Karaev et al., 2024; 2025; Lai et al., 2026). 3D point tracking methods lift pixels with monocular depth and iterative refinement (Xiao et al., 2024), improve dense long-range estimation through optimized surrogate queries (Ngo et al., 2025b;a), or jointly estimate geometry, camera, and object motion (Xiao et al., 2025). GFM-based 4D perceivers represent dynamic 3D scenes through per-frame point maps (Zhang et al., 2025a), dynamic point maps (Sucar et al., 2026), conditional frame-wise decoding (Luo et al., 2026), or motion bases (Lin et al., 2026). Other approaches include common-time point-map pairs (Feng et al., 2025), parametric trajectories (Liu et al., 2026), and scene flow (Zhu et al., 2026; Karhade et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2026). Most rely on frame-aligned grid decoding, coupling output sampling and cost to spatial resolution, whereas D4RT (Zhang et al., 2026a) decouples prediction from predefined grids through on-demand queries. Generative Priors for Geometry and Motion. Large pretrained generators encode geometry and motion priors transferable to perception tasks (Zhan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026). Image adaptations estimate depth through iterative denoising (Ke et al., 2024) or single-step regression (He et al., 2025). This formulation enables direct feature extraction while avoiding the overhead of iterative denoising. Data Usage. We distinguish two types of input frames: encoder frames, which are input to the encoder to extract scene tokens, and query frames, which provide local RGB patches for decoder queries. They share the same aspect ratio but may differ in resolution. Encoder frames are maximally center-cropped to one of five predefined aspect ratios and uniformly resized to the largest resolution within 480 832 bound, while query frames generally retain their original resolution. To speed up training, we use EVAE to pre-encode all video clips into latents and discard the VAE during training. We also apply temporal augmentation to handle varying motion speeds. To this end, each raw video is subsampled into 49-frame clips with temporal intervals ranging from 1 to 4. During training, we randomly slice the first 21 49 frames in steps of 4, and head-truncate the video latent accordingly. We also apply downsizing-only spatial augmentation to the query frames, so that the model sees variety of query-patch fields of view. See Secs. B.1 and B.2 for more details about datasets and data preprocessing & sampling, respectively. Architecture. We evaluate two adaptation variants. The basic variant, denoted as Ours, leverages motion priors from large-scale video generator, with trainable rank-512 4D-LoRA, 512 4D . The double-LoRA variant, denoted as Ours-II, additionally incorporates geometry priors through the frozen rank-512 Depth-LoRA, 512 Depth (Sec. 3.3). Both variants have 0.70B trainable encoder parameters. We use an 8-block cross-attention decoder, which has 0.18B trainable parameters. Optimization. We train for 75K optimization steps using AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) on 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Gradient accumulation yields an effective batch size of 32 video clips. The learning rate is linearly warmed up to peak of 104 over the first 2.5K steps and then follows cosine decay schedule to 106. We apply maximum gradient norm clipping of 10. 4.2 WORLD-COORDINATE TRACKING Evaluation Protocol. We evaluate the performance of 3D tracking on WorldTrack (Feng et al., 2025), which includes Aria Digital Twin (ADT), Dynamic Replica (DR), PointOdyssey (PO), and Panoptic Studio (PS) (Joo et al., 2015). We report results for All and Dynamic points on ADT, DR, and PO, and for all points on PS, whose evaluated tracks are entirely dynamic. Dynamic points are identified by accumulated ground-truth displacements exceeding certain threshold, default set to 5 103 m.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present Gen4P, feed-forward 4D perceiver that processes monocular video input for full 4D reconstruction. The key to its success is to leverage prior knowledge from pretrained video generators in single-step manner, which differs from traditional multi-step denoising-based 4D perceivers. Our on-demand decoder enables flexible spatial and temporal querying, while frozen video-depth LoRA provides plug-in geometry prior without additional trainable parameters. Crucially, we demonstrate

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: that Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art and flexible 4D reconstruction, with future improvement expected as video generative pretraining continues to advance. We also demonstrate its capability to accurately capture dynamic motion and intricate details in real-world videos. Together, these findings support video generators as promising foundation for unified 4D reconstruction.

sections.content: A.1 ADDITIONAL QUALITATIVE RESULTS In Fig. 7, we show additional qualitative results, including merged point clouds, tracking and camera pose estimation, and additional 3D tracking showcases. A.2 CONFIDENCE FILTERING We use the expp1 confidence activation, i.e., = 1 + exp(ˆc) with ˆc denoting the raw confidence output, following VGGT (Wang et al., 2025a). This allows us to apply percentile-based confidence filtering to remove points that the model predicts with low confidence, typically distributed at the far-away background or foreground boundaries. In Fig. 8, we demonstrate an application of confidence filtering. As shown in the Raw column, the direct tracking outputs are already visually clean, but may contain small number of flying points. By applying confidence filtering, with percentile as low as 2%, these flying points can be effectively suppressed, resulting in cleaner foreground and background content. We hereby clarify that for fair comparisons, the visualization results for any method in Fig. 4 and Fig. 6 are NOT applied with confidence-based suppression.

sections.title: B TRAINING PREPARATION
sections.content: B.1 DATASETS We distinguish two types of input frames: encoder frames, which are fed to the encoder to extract scene tokens, and query frames, from which local RGB patches are extracted to construct decoder queries. The two share the same aspect ratio but may differ in spatial resolution. For encoder frames, each raw video is maximally center-cropped to one of five predefined aspect ratios. The cropped frames are then uniformly resized to the largest resolution within 480 832 bound, resulting in five encoder frame sizes: 480 480, 480 640, 480 832, 352 832, and 256 832. The corresponding query frames use the same cropped content before resizing, and their resolutions therefore depend on the native resolution of each dataset. The resulting encoder frame and query frame resolutions are reported in Tab. A1. We preprocess each dataset under these spatial configurations and report the approximate number of resulting subclips for each configuration in the Est. Subclip Count Per Size column. During training, datasets are sampled according to the probabilities reported in the final column. In practice, we tolerate slight distortion between them. To vary the effective field of view of query patches, we apply downsizing-only augmentation to the query frames. For each training clip, we first resize them within 960 1664 bound, then sample side length scale factor from [0.5, 1.0], and resize all query frames by the same factor. This augmentation is applied only to the query frames for the decoder, while the pre-encoded latents remain unchanged. We dont apply random content cropping, color jittering or Gaussian blurring. B.2 PREPROCESSING AND SAMPLING Preprocessing. Each raw video is subsampled into 49-frame clips with frame intervals ranging from 1 to 4. We then pre-encode each clip with the Wan-VAE (Wan et al., 2025) and store the normalized latents. For each clip, camera poses are defined in the first-frame relative world coordinate. The 3D position GT is expressed in the tcam camera coordinate. We adopt mean normalization as in MotionCrafter (Zhu et al., 2026): valid visible 3D GT points are centered and normalized by their mean distance to the origin. Then they are transformed to tcams camera coordinate system. The displacement and normal GTs are represented in the same camera coordinate system.

sections.content: D.1 WORLD-COORDINATE TRACKING Motion Threshold. ADT, DR and PO contain both static and dynamic tracks, whereas PS contains only dynamic tracks. To reliably distinguish dynamic points from static ones for evaluation, we need to select an appropriate motion threshold that suppresses numerical noise in static GT tracks while preserving dynamic tracks with small motions. We measure the motion of each GT track by accumulating adjacent-frame 3D displacements over 64 frames in meters. As shown in Tab. A4, increasing the threshold from 5 103 1 102 changes the average static ratio only marginally from 56.82% 57.29%, indicating that 5 103 is adequate for removing the majority of the numerical noise. In contrast, increasing the threshold from 5 103 5 102 may lead to noticeably more wrongly classified static tracks. The static ratio on ADT shows 67.23% 74.30%, non-negligible 7.07%, while on PStudio, despite being fully dynamic, increases to 2.00%. We therefore use 5 103 as the dynamic-motion threshold throughout our world-coordinate tracking evaluation. Metric Evaluation. We follow the protocol of MonST3R (Zhang et al., 2025a) using the single global median scale alignment to the GT tracks in the frame-0 world coordinate over the 64-frame tracks.
